#2483. Luka Dončić reveals he 'wanted Walker' Kessler, helped push Lakers GM Rob Pelinka for big trade

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The controversial blockbuster trade that sent Walker Kessler to the Los Angeles Lakers this offseason was completed at the request of Luka Dončić, who revealed in an interview with ESPN that he personally asked the team acquire Kessler during a meeting with president and general manager Rob Pelinka.

"I told them after the season I wanted Walker," Dončić said.

"I think he's a really good player," Dončić continued. "Obviously, last season he didn't play. He played like five games. Obviously, [Utah] kept him out, but just playing against him in the previous years, it was hard to score. He was protecting the rim, he was dominating the paint. So just after the season, I went to them and said, 'I want Walker.'"

The Lakers paid a massive price to acquire Kessler:

In addition to the picks, the Lakers gave Kessler a four-year, $130 million deal. At the time, the move was regarded as a big overpay -- CBS Sports' Sam Quinn graded it a C+ in the moment -- especially considering that Kessler played just five games last season due to a torn labrum, and had not played more than 64 games since his rookie season.

However, the general consensus was that it would indeed make the Lakers better, not least of all because it would make Dončić happy -- a fact Dončić confirmed to ESPN.

"When we talked, they told me it's not going to be easy," Dončić said. "I knew that. But when I heard we're going to get him, I was very happy and excited for the season."

Few expected that Kessler's arrival would make the Lakers this good, however. And while there's still a very real world where giving up so much draft capital comes back to bite them, the Lakers have no regrets about the deal while they're sitting in first place in the Western Conference at 15-3.

Kessler has been fantastic in his first month with the Lakers. He's averaging 14 points, 10.8 rebounds, 1.1 steals and 2.1 blocks while shooting 66.9% from the field, including 72.6% in the restricted area. He's ninth in rebounding, third in blocks, and is one of two players (along with Victor Wembanyama) averaging at least one steal and two blocks.

Again, it's still early, but the Lakers have a plus-12.2 net rating in 530 minutes with Kessler on the floor and a minus-0.7 net rating in 339 minutes without him. Kessler has allowed the Lakers to play a more aggressive defensive style because they know they have him waiting at the rim.

As a result, the Lakers are first in opponent turnover rate (18.5%) and allow the seventh-fewest attempts per game in the restricted area (21.7). Just look at the difference in opponents' rim success with and without Kessler:

(Rim frequency = percentage of field goal attempts at the rim)

For all of the questions about the Lakers' defense with a Dončić and Austin Reaves backcourt, the team is 11th in defensive rating (112.4), which is more than good enough to support their dominant offensive attack, led by Dončić's 36.6 points per game.

#2482. Mason Rudolph and Steelers defense can clean up Aaron Rodgers' mess, but the franchise's problems run deeper

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Well, of course Mason Rudolph was the answer.

Days after Aaron Rodgers set fire to the place on his way out of town, the Steelers turned to the same quarterback who rescued their season three years ago. And against a Broncos team that came to Pittsburgh with eight wins and legitimate Super Bowl aspirations, the Steelers were unequivocally the better football team.

So now what? Is this a dead-cat-bounce win for a team that just endured Aaron Rodgers Armageddon, or is there something here? And if the Broncos can entertain thoughts of winning a Super Bowl with what they've gotten out of Bo Nix this season, why can't the Steelers make something of their remaining season with Rudolph?

And after all that's happened, the Steelers are somehow 7-4. If you squint, there are reasons to believe they can make something of this season. There are also reasons, if you're clear-headed and rational, to be concerned about what another nine- or 10-win season might mean for an organization that has spent years mistaking winning for progress.

Maybe the Steelers found a way to salvage a season that, 48 hours ago, felt unsalvageable. What they can't afford to do is mistake that for having figured out their future.

We've previously written about the Broncos, whose ability to win close games has been unprecedented. They've done it despite routinely getting outgained and despite uneven play from Nix.

But here's the thing: Coming into their Black Friday matchup, the Steelers had played better defense than the Broncos, hadn't been outgained by anything close to 700 yards and hadn't needed nearly as many late-game heroics to win. The Broncos had two more victories to show for it, but there wasn't nearly as much separating these teams as their records might suggest.

Nix had been playing considerably better of late. After an underwhelming first six games, he was averaging 52 more passing yards per game and had thrown six touchdowns against two interceptions over his next four starts. Denver won all four games, scoring at least 26 points each time.

Friday served as a reminder of just how much Denver needs Nix to take care of the football. One of his greatest strengths coming into the season was his ability to avoid sacks, which helped offset his inability to consistently generate big plays. The Steelers defense turned a Nix sack-fumble and a pick-six into 14 points in the first half alone. When it was over, Patrick Graham's group had sacked Nix twice and held him to 169 passing yards with no touchdowns and two interceptions.

Pittsburgh has a defense capable of doing that to opposing QBs. The question, as it has been for the better part of eight seasons, is whether the Steelers' own quarterback situation can overcome replacement-level play.

Nobody's confusing Rudolph with anything more than a reliable journeyman backup. They need him to be better than Aaron Rodgers, which, despite everything Rodgers accomplished in his first two decades in the league, was immediately obvious on Friday.

And it's worth remembering what Rudolph did the last time the Steelers found themselves in such a predicament. In his three regular-season starts in 2023, he averaged more than 10 yards per attempt, threw three touchdowns without an interception and won all three games. Nobody benefited more from Rudolph's willingness to push the ball downfield than George Pickens.

Reprising the role of Pickens on Friday: DK Metcalf!

On Friday, Rudolph completed 9 of 15 passes for 142 yards, including a 58-yarder to rookie Germie Bernard, a 37-yarder to Roman Wilson and a 22-yard touchdown to the aforementioned Mr. Metcalf. Given what the Steelers have invested in their wide receivers and how little they've gotten in return, it'll be worth watching whether Rudolph can consistently get more out of that group than Rodgers did.

If Rudolph can do for the Steelers what he did back in '23, it's reasonable to think that, yes, this group will make the playoffs – and, yes, will be underdogs to actually win a playoff game. The bigger concern, however, is how the organization might interpret that success given the last decade.

Because we've been here before. Three years ago, the Steelers were 6-4, had set the forward-passing game back decades, and eventually turned to Mason Rudolph to save their season. Since then, they've changed coordinators and head coaches, completely overhauled their quarterback room (twice), and committed $209 million to two of the NFL's least productive wide receivers (whether due to injury or inconsistency).

And what do they have to show for it? Consider this: Of the 133 NFL teams to start 6-4 since 2000, only three were less efficient throwing the football than the '26 Steelers: the 2000 Lions, the 2022 Jets and … the aforementioned 2023 Steelers (as measured by EPA per dropback).

Expand that group to include seven previous teams that started 6-4 and also really struggled to throw the ball, and here's what happened: Not a single, solitary one of them improved its record the following season. In fact, together they won just 35% of their games, and four of those seven lost at least 12 times.

And what did those franchises do in the seasons that followed? Some found their way out of the dysfunction; others made decisions that would haunt them for years—and, in some cases, decades.

6-4 teams with struggling passing offenses, 2000-25

Teams since 2000 that started 6-4 with an EPA/dropback of -0.07 or worse.

In 2003, four years removed from Dan Marino's retirement, Miami had Ricky Williams in the backfield and a defense that featured Jason Taylor, Zach Thomas, Junior Seau, Patrick Surtain and Sam Madison. Dave Wannstedt's team won 10 games with Jay Fiedler and Brian Griese at quarterback. The Dolphins missed the playoffs, but it's not difficult to understand why they might have thought they were a quarterback away.

They traded a future second-round pick for AJ Feeley, who threw 15 interceptions in eight starts in 2004. Williams abruptly retired, Wannstedt resigned and the Dolphins won four games. Enter Nick Saban, who got them back to 9-7 in his first season with Gus Frerotte.

And then came perhaps the most consequential personnel decision of the century for the Dolphins: In March 2006, Miami passed on Drew Brees, who was coming off shoulder surgery, and traded a second-round pick for Daunte Culpepper, who was recovering from a serious knee injury.

Saban has since said he wanted Brees, but the Dolphins' doctors wouldn't clear him. Either way, Culpepper started four games for Miami, Brees spent the next 15 seasons in New Orleans, and Saban was in Tuscaloosa less than a year later. The Dolphins went 1-15 in 2007.

Then there's Detroit, which replaced longtime executive Chuck Schmidt with Matt Millen following its nine-win season in 2000. Millen hired Marty Mornhinweg; the Lions won two games, and a year later they drafted Joey Harrington with the third overall pick. Detroit drafted a wide receiver in the first round in each of the next three years: Charles Rogers, Roy Williams and Mike Williams.

The Lions went 31-97 from 2001-2008, including a 0-16 finish in Millen's final season.

They finally got it right at quarterback, drafting Matthew Stafford first overall in 2009, but went 74-90-1 in his starts over 12 seasons and never won a playoff game. Stafford won a Super Bowl in his first season after Detroit traded him to the Rams in 2021, and the Lions finally figured it out after hiring GM Brad Holmes and head coach Dan Campbell. With Jared Goff, Detroit went from three wins in 2021 to nine in 2022 to 12 and an NFC Championship game appearance in 2023. Detroit won more playoff games that season (two) than it had in the previous 65 seasons combined (one).

The 2022 Jets had the NFL's fourth-ranked scoring defense, both the Offensive and Defensive Rookies of the Year in Garrett Wilson and Sauce Gardner … and a problem at quarterback. Former No. 2 overall pick Zach Wilson didn't come close to living up to his draft status, and Robert Saleh's team went 1-6 down the stretch.

General manager Joe Douglas traded for Rodgers, the Jets hired Nathaniel Hackett as offensive coordinator and brought in some of Rodgers' former teammates. Rodgers tore his Achilles in the opener, New York won seven games – just as they had the season before – and they doubled down the following offseason, eventually trading for Davante Adams.

The Jets did improve throwing the football in 2024. The defense, meanwhile, went from one of the league's best to a liability. They won five games, fired Saleh and Douglas, moved on from Rodgers and won three games in 2025.

This should sound familiar. One difference: Gardner, Wilson, Quinnen Williams and Breece Hall were all 25 or younger when New York first decided they were just a QB away. Pittsburgh doesn't have that luxury with T.J. Watt, Cameron Heyward and Jalen Ramsey.

Bill O'Brien's Texans won exactly nine games in each of his first three seasons as head coach. Houston gave Brock Osweiler $72 million in 2016; he threw more interceptions than touchdowns, and general manager Rick Smith spent the following offseason getting himself out of the mess.

The Texans attached a second-round pick to Osweiler to get Cleveland to take his contract, then gave the Browns two first-rounders to move from No. 25 to No. 12 to draft Deshaun Watson. Watson tore his ACL as a rookie, but Houston won 21 games and two division titles over the next two seasons.

Tennessee didn't have to spend nearly as much. The Titans parted ways with Mike Mularkey after winning a playoff game in January 2018, hired Mike Vrabel and, a year later, GM Jon Robinson got to work.

He traded for Ryan Tannehill, ostensibly to back up Marcus Mariota, signed guard Rodger Saffold and drafted Jeffery Simmons, AJ Brown and four-year starting guard Nate Davis with his first three picks. Vrabel promoted Arthur Smith to offensive coordinator, Tannehill replaced Mariota in October of the '19 season and the Titans were playing for a trip to the Super Bowl three months later.

The other example is New England, which appeared to have found Tom Brady's successor in Mac Jones, the 15th overall pick in 2021. Jones made the Pro Bowl and led the Patriots to the playoffs as a rookie before Bill Belichick, in a peculiar display of hubris, entrusted his offense to a longtime defensive coordinator (Matt Patricia) and his young quarterback's development to a former special teams coordinator (Joe Judge). Jones never recovered in New England, and both he and Kenny Pickett, whom the Steelers drafted 20th overall a year later, were traded in March 2024.

The Patriots endured consecutive four-win seasons, drafted Drake Maye third overall, hired Vrabel and Josh McDaniels, and added Will Campbell, TreVeyon Henderson and Stefon Diggs. They won 14 games in 2025 and went to the Super Bowl.

So what exactly are the Steelers building?

Really, the Steelers have been trying to solve some variation of the same problem since 2019, when Ben Roethlisberger suffered a season-ending elbow injury in Week 2. In six of the eight seasons since, they've had a below-average offense through 10 games, and in five of those seasons, their passing game actually cost them points (at least as measured by EPA per dropback).

Perhaps Mike Tomlin's greatest accomplishment over his final seven seasons in Pittsburgh was his ability to hold together a team that was frequently overmatched offensively. Whatever your criticisms of Tomlin -- and there were plenty of legitimate ones -- there's something to be said for consistently winning with the quarterbacks he had. McCarthy inherited many of those same problems, and we're beginning to see what happens when the head coach can no longer paper over them.

We've written plenty about Pittsburgh's recent struggles in the draft, the decision to pay DK Metcalf $150 million and trade George Pickens and whether the organization's obsession with avoiding a losing season has done more long-term harm than short-term good.

They're not unrelated. The organization spent recent years making personnel decisions as if it had the franchise QB on the roster. They've committed big money to veteran receivers, and four players they selected in the first three rounds from 2022 through 2025 -- Pickett, George Pickens, Broderick Jones and Kaleb Johnson -- have all been traded away.

GM Omar Khan has drafted some good young players, but how much longer can Pittsburgh operate under the assumption that it's only a competent quarterback away from winning its first playoff game since the 2016 season?

The last time Pittsburgh had a losing season? It was 2003, and a few months later, it drafted Ben Roethlisberger. That doesn't mean another losing season guarantees another Big Ben, any more than drafting Joey Harrington guaranteed Detroit anything.

And there's nothing wrong with Rudolph helping this team win 10 games. There is something wrong with using that as justification for another offseason of the same decisions that got us here in the first place.

But the danger isn't going 6-11. As we wrote back in January, after Tomlin retired, the Steelers entered the offseason with the NFL's second-oldest roster, $46.6 million in cap space and 12 draft picks. It was an opportunity to get younger, accumulate more draft capital by moving some veteran players and build a roster capable of supporting their next franchise QB. Instead, the Steelers doubled down on winning now despite little evidence they were close to winning anything meaningful. The danger is continuing to operate as if they're close to winning a Super Bowl when they're much closer to being a bad football team with an expensive roster and no quarterback.

The Dolphins thought they were a quarterback away, too. That was more than 20 years ago, and they're still waiting to win another playoff game.

#2479. Black Friday scorigami: Steelers-Broncos ends with final score that's never happened before in NFL history

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Pittsburgh Steelers dealt with plenty of drama this week, but that didn't seem to slow them down on Black Friday. The Steelers destroyed the Broncos 27-5, and in the process, they made some history: This marked the first time in the NFL's 107-year history that a game has ever ended with that exact final score.

The final points came in the fourth quarter when Chris Boswell hit a 33-yard field goal. That was a huge kick, because if he had missed it, a final score of 24-5 would NOT have been a scorigami, but Boswell's kick went through, and that ultimately gave us the 1,102nd final score in NFL history.

DEN 5 - PIT 27🚨 SCORIGAMI 🚨That is the 1102nd unique score in NFL history, and the 7th of the 2026 season. pic.twitter.com/HHAt6TjtjB

This game featured a rare double scorigami: The Steelers led 24-5 after two quarters, marking the first time in NFL history that particular halftime score had ever occurred.

For a game to end in a scorigami, you need a few bizarre things to happen, and that was certainly the case here. The biggest thing that helped the scorigami happen was that the Broncos recorded a safety in the second quarter, making the score 14-2.

SAFETY 🚨DENvsPIT on Prime VideoStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/PCvKd7Cgze

The Broncos then tacked on a Wil Lutz field goal later in the second quarter, but with Bo Nix struggling, the offense didn't score a single point for the rest of the game. When one team finishes a game with exactly five points, you're almost guaranteed to get a scorigami, and that's what happened here.

The Broncos were the first team to finish with exactly five points since 2021, when the Cardinals lost a game 31-5 to the Texans (That game was also a scorigami). This game marked the first time in three years that the Broncos were involved in a scorigami. The last instance came back in November 2023 in a 29-12 loss to the Browns.

On the Steelers' end, there was nothing bizarre about their point total, but their defense deserves a lot of credit for making this scorigami happen. Not only did T.J. Watt score on a fumble-return touchdown in the first quarter, but Jalen Ramsey also tacked on a pick-six in the second quarter. On top of that, the Steelers' defense had a suffocating performance against Denver, holding the Broncos out of the end zone.

The Aaron Rodgers situation might have caused some drama in Pittsburgh this week, but there was no drama in this game.

Pittsburgh's win marks the second time this month the Steelers have been involved in a scorigami. Back in Week 10, their 38-18 loss to the Bengals also made history as the first time a final score had never happened before. The Steelers are now one of four teams this year — along with the Bengals, Cowboys, and Titans — involved in multiple scorigamis.

Overall, there have been seven scorigamis this year, which is already more than we saw during the entire 2025 season (five). It's also more than we saw in 2024, when there were six in total. This is turning into the year of the scorigami.

#2478. Former lottery pick Rob Dillingham sucker-punched in G League game, leading to scrum, multiple ejections

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former No. 8 overall pick Rob Dillingham was sucker-punched by Felix Okpara during a G League game between the Westchester Knicks and Capital City Go-Go on Friday afternoon. Dillingham and Okpara were both ejected after the incident, which turned into a full-on scrum that spilled off the court.

Dillingham, who was traded to the New York Knicks' G League affiliate earlier this month, pushed Okpara in the chest as the two were running up the floor early in the fourth quarter. Okpara looked around to see if an official had seen what happened, waited a few seconds, then unleashed a haymaker on Dillingham.

Former lottery pick and now Westchester #Knicks PG Rob Dillingham punched by Capital City GoGo big man Felix Okpara Thankfully, Ermal Kuqo - the WestChester Knicks front office exec, who separated hot heads, is 6-10 and 270 lbs pic.twitter.com/wg1FbELQyq

Dillingham was knocked down, but got to his feet quickly and chased after Okpara, who retreated immediately. Players, officials, coaches, team executives and security all rushed in to separate the two, and the situation eventually calmed down without any further issues.

Both players are likely to face additional punishment beyond their ejections. Okpara, in particular, is almost certainly facing a suspension.

The Minnesota Timberwolves traded an unprotected 2031 first-round pick and a 2030 pick swap to the San Antonio Spurs for the No. 8 overall pick in the 2024 NBA Draft, which they used to select Dillingham out of the University of Kentucky, where he had an impressive freshman season.

Dillingham, 21, never got much of a chance in Minnesota, however, in large part because the Timberwolves were trying to contend -- they went to the Western Conference Finals in his rookie season -- and weren't in a position to let him play through mistakes. He played just 84 games in a season and a half with the Timberwolves before he was traded to the Chicago Bulls as part of the Ayo Dosunmu deal.

In 30 games with the Bulls, Dillingham got a much bigger opportunity, but failed to impress. He averaged 9.6 points on 50.3% true shooting in 21.5 minutes, and had an 18.3% turnover rate. Notably, he shot just 30% from 3-point range, when outside shooting was supposed to be one of his primary strengths coming out of college.

The Bulls traded Dillingham to the Charlotte Hornets for Buddy Hield in September ahead of training camp, and the Hornets waived him a day later.

On Nov. 13, the Westchester Knicks acquired the returning player rights to Dillingham from the Iowa Wolves, in exchange for the returning player rights to Tuburu Naivalurua, Westchester's own future first-round pick and a 2027 second-round pick in the G League Draft.

Dillingham put up 26 points and six assists on 10 of 18 from the field, including 3 of 5 from 3-point range, in his debut on Nov. 20. Entering Friday's contest, he was averaging 21 points and 6.3 assists, while shooting 35.3% from behind the arc.

"I ain't really trying to show too much of anything to anyone or prove to anyone, it's more internal - showing myself that I can play basketball at the highest level, fit into any situation and help.I want everyone to see that I'm better at these things, for sure, but that's… https://t.co/MriaFDFX9w pic.twitter.com/lAFXQROU0x

"I ain't really trying to show too much of anything to anyone or prove to anyone, it's more internal," Dillingham told SNY ahead of his debut. "Showing myself that I can play basketball at the highest level, fit into any situation and help.

"I want everyone to see that I'm better at these things, for sure, but that's not my goal. If you focus on that, then you're going to lose focus on what you're really trying to do. Focused on myself, getting better, so when I get the opportunity, I'm ready and improved."

#2477. The Timing Game – MH

von Next Generation am 31.03.2025 in den Kategorien Tactical Theory mit 1 Kommentar

The Timing Game describes a playing philosophy in which the right moment of an action is crucial. It not only allows pressing traps to be reversed but also enables teams to break down deep defensive blocks with precision. In the Premier League, Brighton’s then-manager Roberto De Zerbi took this tactical approach to a new level.

“Brighton is a master of passing the ball to the free man but recognising when to pass the ball to the free man and moving at the right time.” – Pep Guardiola

The core idea of the Timing Game is to react to the opponent’s movement at precisely the right moment. Pressing traps can be reversed by first triggering and manipulating the opponent’s press and then bypassing it through changes in speed and direction. Since opposition pressing actions are highly dynamic, this approach is particularly effective against high-pressing teams. Consequently, the Timing Game allows teams to dominate pressing situations in their own buildup play. Additionally, because opponent movements can be triggered independently of the game phase, the Timing Game can also be applied against deep defensive blocks.

Regarding the role of timing in De Zerbi’s buildup play, René Maric (RM) explained in a 2023 interview with SkySports:

„The biggest thing in the build-up is the control of rhythm. If you look at Guardiola, he does it with the speed of the passes and then they carry the ball when they don’t have pressure. De Zerbi does it more with the moment of the pass, the lure, the sole on the ball, opening space with the pass rather than the carry. How you control the rhythm and progress through space will be big in the future. That development has already started.“

This article examines the dimensions and functioning of the Timing Game. Additionally, it analyzes the impact of a team’s own positioning, as well as the manipulation, anticipation, and triggering of the opponent’s press (or movements). The following sections will then explore the action of bypassing the opponent, the potential issues that arise within the Timing Game, and possible solutions to these challenges.

This section is an attempt to highlight the various facets of the Timing Game and football in general. Different playing philosophies prioritize different dimensions. In the Timing Game described here, particular focus is placed on the timing of dynamics in relation to the opponent.

To gain a better understanding of the principles of the Timing Game, the following section presents and explains its different dimensions. This makes it clear how the Timing Game differs from the focus of positional play and relationism but can also be combined with them. Although the game dimensions are less important for the practical implementation of the Timing Game, they can be useful for further developing this concept or other coaching philosophies.

The most important dimension of the Timing Game is the temporal dimension. The crucial factors are the speed and timing of decision-making. The timing of a progressive action should generally coincide with the opponent’s movement. The primary focus is therefore on the exact moment of an action.

A second important dimension is that of dynamics. The dynamic dimension of the Timing Game revolves around explosiveness and changes in rhythm. Changes in dynamics can be decisive both in relation to one’s own play and in terms of directional shifts in relation to the opponent. Ultimately, the goal is to create the strongest possible reciprocal acceleration in the opponent.

In the dimension of individual performance factors, the focus is on footballing competencies such as technical and athletic abilities. In the Timing Game, ball control is a crucial factor, as it significantly affects a player’s pressing resistance. Ball control involves both the ability to recognize a situation and the technical capability to handle the ball under pressure at any time. This skill is particularly important in the Timing Game, as it provides an advantage during the opponent’s pressing phase.

The causal-relational dimension deals with the cause-and-effect principle in interactions between teammates and opponents. There is a causal relationship both between the opponent’s defensive approach and the method of bypassing them, as well as between a teammate’s action and the resulting ball action. The following examples illustrate this:

In relationism, interactions between teammates are particularly emphasized to enable optimal interplay. Due to the complexity of this dimension, I have linked MR’s seminar “The Future of the Game” here.

In the spatial dimension, the focus is on controlling specific zones of the pitch. This is particularly crucial in positional play, where the aim is to control the game through ball possession and spatial occupation. In the Timing Game, however, the goal is to reach the space behind the opponent. Since this space is constantly changing, it cannot strictly be defined as a fixed pitch zone. However, the spatial dimension does play a role in the preparatory positioning of the Timing Game. This article contains a dedicated section on the optimal positioning in preparation for the Timing Game.

In the Timing Game, the moment of an action is primarily decisive. The moment of action is always triggered by the opponent’s movement. The more intense the opponent’s movement, the easier it is to bypass them. This is because, once the Timing Game is triggered, the opponent should be bypassed as diagonally opposed to their movement as possible. This forces the opponent into a maximal change of direction and dynamics.

The pressing near one’s own penalty area is bypassed diagonally opposite to the direction of the press.

A temporal advantage is created over the opponent, who initially has to accelerate in the opposite direction and loses time. The space that opens up behind the advancing opponent can be played most effectively. Representing the functioning of the Timing Game, the principle of “Lure and Shock” could be used. The opponent is first “lured” into the movement and then “shocked” by being bypassed.

The Timing Game is particularly effective during the opponent’s transition from a deeper to a higher pressing setup. At the moment of transition between ordered pressing phases, the opponent’s structure is often lacking, as the distances between the players change. Additionally, movement is present on all positions of the opponent, which can be exploited for the Timing Game. The direction of the opponent’s movement is also crucial, as during the transition from a deeper to a higher pressing phase, vertical movement away from the goal dominates, allowing spaces towards the opponent’s goal to be exploited.

This specific moment of the opponent’s pressing transition into a higher setup cannot be found in the classic phase model of the game according to Van Gaal. Depending on the perspective, it would be classified as part of either the team’s own possession phase or the opponent’s possession phase, even though it is significantly more complex and interesting than other possession situations. The opponent is essentially in a type of defensive transition into attack from the opponent’s ball possession, while the own team takes advantage of this moment and transitions from their own ball possession into a kind of offensive transition.

The Timing Game, however, does not only work during transitions between different pressing setups, but also independently of the game phase, and thus also within the framework of the opponent’s attacking press. The opponent’s movement in attacking pressing usually does not need to be triggered additionally. Instead, it is more about anticipating the moment when the opponent’s attacking press is triggered. At the moment of pressing initiation, there is a very high dynamic on multiple positions of the opponent in (diagonal) vertical directions, which allows the pressing to be bypassed with suitable movements at the moment of initiation. Particularly, the opponent’s pressing traps can be bypassed at the moment of initiation through a corresponding pre-rehearsed anticipation and movement.

Depending on the individual pressing patterns of the opponent, preparations should be made for the timing and manner of bypassing. For example, man-marking in attacking pressing can be bypassed differently than ball-oriented or hybrid marking schemes. Particularly against man-marking, it is important in the Timing Game to initially provoke dynamics in the opponent through various runs, in order to then bypass them in the opposite direction. If dynamics are not created through own runs, there is often little movement from the opponent in the second and third layers that could be exploited.

Because dynamics are also created in the opponent’s man-marking in the second and third layers, multiple layers can be bypassed.

The pressing triggers and pressing traps also differ depending on the type of attacking press, so anticipating the moments of the Timing Game requires prior analysis of the opponent. A very commonly used pressing trigger is a backward pass to the goalkeeper from a higher defensive line. A common reaction is for the goalkeeper to play the ball long under pressure, usually resulting in a loss of possession. In the Timing Game, a team would create passing options behind the opponent through collective movements at the moment the opponent triggers their press. Specific movements and methods for bypassing the press will be discussed in more detail later in the article.

Individual pressing patterns also include the opponent’s pressing structure itself. Here too, individual weaknesses can be diagnosed and exploited in advance. When the opponent presses from a 4-4-2, they often have an under-populated central area. Of course, this cannot be generalized, as, for example, the ball-far midfielder or an aggressive center-back may situationally reinforce the center. However, if this is not the case, an inverse run by the full-back at the moment the press is triggered could be useful to play into the space behind the press against the dynamics. It can be stated that the Timing Game, against different opponents with different individual pressing patterns, influences the movements made to bypass the press.

The Timing Game can also work against deep-lying opponents. However, it is more difficult here because, in general, there is less movement away from the goal, and the opponent attacks in a more passive manner. The deep-lying opponent’s goal is to close the space near the goal. It will be crucial to trigger the opponent’s movement or pressing and lure the opponent out. We will go into more detail on such trigger actions later.

In summary, the following rules for the Timing Game depending on the opponent’s pressing can be established: The deeper the opponent is positioned, the less dynamic movement there is away from their own goal. Therefore, the time window for bypassing the press is shorter. The more passive the opponent acts, the less frequently there is opponent movement. As a result, there will be fewer opportunities to bypass the press. Nevertheless, the Timing Game can be used independently of the game phase through trigger actions.

The team’s formation in possession should be adapted to the challenges of the Timing Game. It should create central connections through a vertical/diagonal alignment. This way, more layers can be incorporated into the dynamics, and more passing options can be created. More passing windows open up at the moment of triggering through a variety of passing angles. In the event of a loss of possession, it also allows for more effective counter-pressing.

Additionally, it can be useful to work with asymmetries and overloads. Overloading the own buildup zone is particularly effective when the opponent closes down and applies high pressure. This lures the opponent and allows them to be bypassed with a few passes. In the linked video example, De Zerbi’s Shakhtar Donetsk uses a strategy of having 7 players in their own penalty area during a goal kick to lure the opponent out.

Nothing to see here, just a completely normal build-up pic.twitter.com/vOcvRPVKdf

— Jamie Hamilton (@stirling_j) April 28, 2022

Problems in the Timing Game arise when there is an overload in the own buildup zone if the opponent does not press. The progression in the game is lacking because offensive passing options are not available. Also problematic is the static overload of the last line. If players remain in their specific spaces in the last line, passing options necessary to bypass the opponent’s press are missing.

Another way to structure the team to prepare for the Timing Game is by leaving a specific area vacant. If the opponent attempts to press, this space is usually left unoccupied by the opponent as well. Subsequently, the space can be attacked and played into from the second line in the opposite direction. If the space is still occupied, the numerical advantage in a ball-near area can be exploited. Real Madrid often employs such structures or space-drawing runs in preparation for their actual attacking play with the ball.

In the Timing Game, the moment the opponent begins to press must be anticipated as early as possible. Possible indicators for early recognition of a pressing moment include: the opponent’s approach towards the ball-carrying teammate, the shrinking of distances between the ball-near opponents and their teammates, and the forward dynamics of the opponent. A defensive line with equal numbers or an advancing defender is also an early recognition feature. Lastly, specific pressing triggers should be identified through video analysis in advance.

An exemplary player for effective pressing resistance is Sergio Busquets, who, with his excellent ball control, was regularly able to anticipate and resolve pressing situations. In this 2017 article, TR and MR wrote about Busquets’ qualities.

What is particularly interesting is triggering the opponent’s attacking press. There are a variety of very interesting trigger actions. One variation used by De Zerbi is the use of the sole on the ball to wait. This plays on the impatience of the opponent. The following quote and video clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of this trigger action.

“It’s so fascinating to watch (…) when the ball goes to the center back, they freeze the game. (…) As soon as the pressing action happened, they then had this meticulously designed mechanism of up-back-throughs and third man connections (…).” – Jamie Hamilton, 3rd Circle Podcast

— Jamie Hamilton (@stirling_j) January 13, 2025

Another option is a pass triggered by speed. This pass should be played as slowly as possible and as quickly as necessary. The slow pass provokes the opponent’s pressing. At the same time, by the receiver moving towards the ball, the dynamics can immediately be reversed. This facilitates the transition into the action of bypassing or dribbling past the opponent. The pass direction should ideally be diagonal toward one’s own goal. This maximizes the reversal of dynamics.

Another approach is to play into the pressure, only to then “bounce” back into the direction of the opponent’s pressing path. The opponent is initially led to believe they have access by playing into the pressure. By bouncing the ball into the pressing direction, the opponent is forced to continue their run.

The classic way of forcing a passive opponent into movement is dribbling. The opponent is eventually made to press. However, it is also much harder to generate a dynamic shift and surprise effect, as the dribbling is already in the direction of play. Therefore, it is helpful if dribbling-skilled players attack the opponent in order to maintain the unpredictability of the next action with quick changes of direction. Alternatively, passes that bypass the opponent after dribbling in the opposite direction of the dribble path can create a dynamic shift in the opponent.

Against deep-lying opponents, the inside diagonal is a good method to force defenders on the last line to step out a few meters. When the ball is played diagonally from the outside to the center, the central defender steps out a few steps. This can be exploited in the opposite direction. The effect is enhanced by a player letting the ball pass, as immediately after, the defender’s back can be attacked. This move is known in relationism as Escadinha.

After the pressing trigger, the opponent should be bypassed through dynamic, diagonal directional changes. The direction of the first action should ideally not move away from the pressure but rather target, go over, or through it to attack the opponent’s movement. Instead of directly passing to the free player (e.g., the goalkeeper), a progressive, diagonal ball should be chosen.

To create passing options in the desired direction, specific movements are crucial. There are also various fundamental principles for this. The start of the ball action should be as late as possible but as early as necessary.

The timing of the movement of teammates should coincide with the moment the press begins, so they can be available to receive the ball under pressure, but not too early to avoid being caught by the opponent’s dynamic.

Dynamic movement should also be generated in the second and third layers to have the opportunity to bypass multiple layers. Otherwise, there is a risk of opponents from the second layer, who create covering shadows, not being affected by the opposing dynamic. In a less compact space behind the first pressing line, the dynamics can occur in stages, so the layers are played one after the other.

It is important that after an action, the next layer should be attacked immediately to maintain the dynamic.

The decisive action to overcome the opponent can be individual, group, or team tactical in nature. Below are specific examples of such actions.

A feint in the moment of pressing initiation can lead to bypassing the opponent. In the linked video, Musiala’s movement at the right moment leads to the goal. Although this movement is likely executed intuitively by Musiala at the right time, it can certainly be tactically repeated. The feint falls into the above-described phase of the pressing transition from a deeper to a higher pressing line, which is why Denmark’s player spacing is incorrect and the deep coverage is absent.

Brilliant angle of Jamal Musiala’s goal from last night. 🇩🇪#Germany #Denmark #Euro #Analysis pic.twitter.com/xl2MDgvXwb

Individually tactical, the first touch can be used both as a triggering action and as an overcoming action. By skillfully triggering the opponent’s movement, it may be enough to simply play the ball past the opponent or through their legs. The first touch is made as far as possible but as close as necessary to allow the player to regain possession of the ball immediately in front of the opponent. This is clearly seen at the very beginning of Woltemade’s first goal in the following video.

⚽#woltemade #u21 pic.twitter.com/mpdKiB4inJ

The no-look pass can also be a variant to surprise the opponent against the dynamics and running direction.

Florian Wirtz’s dribbles may initially seem unremarkable. However, upon closer observation, it becomes clear that Wirtz uses slight delays instead of flashy tricks to trigger the opponent’s movement, and then he moves the ball past the defender. This is also a form of timing play at the individual tactical level.

— thomassist (@thomassist25_) January 27, 2025

On the group tactical level, up-back-through (steil-klatsch) combinations are ideal for breaking into depth at the right moment. Here, the previously described positioning in preparation for the timing play is crucial. As many levels as possible should be occupied to open passing angles and options. The lay-off play has the advantage of being able to overcome the opponent with simple passes. It is remarkable how each of these passes is played against the opponent’s pressing direction, preventing the opponent from getting access to the ball.

— ファンキーヤング (@funkyyoung) November 19, 2024

Different variations of the play through the third man are also very effective. In the following video, the effectiveness can be admired at minute 0:13, using the example of the left center-back starting in the wrong direction.

Other possibilities in the group tactical area include one-twos against the dynamics, space-creating runs, counter movements, or dynamic zone rotations.

There are also team tactical variations for overcoming the opponent in the timing game. One such variation is playing the second ball directly into the backline with an appropriate zone overload at the moment the pressing is triggered. The preparatory positioning is the team tactical element here.

A team tactical counter movement could also be considered, where all players in the forward zones drop back, increasing the pressing distance to create more dynamic movement. At the same time, a player from the second line attacks deeply in the opposite direction.

One problem with the timing play is overcoming the covering shadow of the first pressing opponent. As the approaching opponent generates an increasingly larger covering shadow in a well-prepared pressing situation, passing options become limited. This can be solved through an individual tactical overcoming action, such as a dribble, a first touch, or others. Additionally, certain combination plays can help overcome the first pressing player. A back-up-back-through combination could be effective, where the first pass is played over a short distance to a nearby teammate (back), followed by an up-back-through combination to open new passing angles.

The short back pass to the goalkeeper, who has moved up into the defensive line, can bypass the covering shadow of the first pressing player.

Another problem could arise against teams with a very high pressing intensity. Since it is necessary to play into the pressure and trigger the pressing, one is systematically exposed to this high intensity repeatedly. However, this can also be used to one’s advantage. Opponents with high intensity also have high dynamics, which can be played against with greater effectiveness. Additionally, there is usually a high number of opponents in the attacking zones. Therefore, it is advisable to attack the farthest free space as directly as possible.

Hybrid pressing can also cause problems in the timings game. Since individual players act in specific spaces, responding situationally to regain possession of the ball, they do not necessarily carry the dynamics of the pressing players. As a result, they are more difficult to play past. However, certain off-ball runs could provide solutions here. One example would be the outside defender making a diagonal run into space far from the ball.

Lastly, there are issues when pressing the opponent during goal kicks. All playing philosophies face problems here, as the conditions to break out of the situation are not ideal. The ball is not in motion, the opponent can organize, and the playing field is limited by the goal line behind. Additionally, the risk is higher due to the proximity to the goal. The timings game would generate dynamics in the opponent by various runs from teammates, in order to reach the opponent’s back at the right moment.

The concept of dynamically timing a play to exploit the opponent’s movement at the right moment is already seen in practice. However, with a more deliberate approach, it can become more accessible to a wider range of players and even more effective. It holds the potential to bypass pressing traps and break down deep-lying defenses. It is not only applicable throughout the field but can also be effective with different numbers of players.

The dynamic timing play concept developed here is heavily focused on the reference point of the “opponent.” Another possible concept of timing could place more emphasis on the teammate, focusing on relational interactions between players. This concept would be more closely aligned with the relationalism theory. Using the dimensions outlined here, different game concepts can be created and further developed.

The timing play should be used as a complementary element to complete one’s overall playing philosophy. It provides a different perspective on tactical analysis than what would be possible with static graphics, such as those on a tactic board. Therefore, it should expand an analyst’s perspective on this complex game by adding an additional dimension.

Author: MH is a football aficionado at heart. His apartment resembles a football library, with shelves filled with books on the great tacticians from Rinus Michels to Pep Guardiola. Of course, the book from Spielverlagerung.de is not missing. For MH, football is not just a game, it’s a way of life. He can be found on X under Mh_sv5 and LinkedIn.

I know Pep Guardiola made De Zerbi the leading authority when it comes to the timing game but I also believe that Marcelino Garcia at Villarreal adds more layers to this topic. His understanding of dynamics is unique and is worth looking into.

#2476. Chargers poised to start DJ Uiagalelei with Justin Herbert ruled out for Week 12

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Just when the Los Angeles Chargers finally build a hint of offensive momentum in their catastrophically disappointing season, they may lose their starting quarterback for at least one game. Justin Herbert will not play in Week 12 against the New England Patriots as he works through the NFL concussion protocol. According to CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz, it is increasingly likely that DJ Uiagalelei will suit up as the starter on Sunday.

Jake Browning is also on the roster, but Uiagalelei is in line to make his first professional start. The Chargers signed Browning, a career backup, to their practice squad in October and inked a contract on Thursday that elevated him to the active roster.

Uiagalelei signed with the Chargers as an undrafted free agent in 2025 and made his first appearance earlier this season, throwing seven passes in the final minutes of a 44-22 loss to the Houston Texans. Uiagalelei completed two of those throws for 24 yards and his first career touchdown.

Although Uiagalelei was once a renowned prospect and began his college career at Clemson as a five-star recruit and the No. 2 overall player in the 2020 class, per 247Sports, he underperformed on expectations and went undrafted after making stops at Oregon State and Florida State. Uiagalelei showed flashes of the high-end playmaker he was supposed to be during his lone season at Oregon State but regressed upon transferring to Florida State and missed much of his final season with a broken finger.

Most of Uiagalelei's professional experience has come in preseason appearances. He played in all three games of the 2025 and 2026 preseasons and completed 55.8% of his throws for 585 yards, four touchdowns and an interception.

This marks a potential new low for a Chargers team that has been a disaster on offense in 2026. With Herbert in the lineup, they ranked 31st in scoring, 26th in yards per game, and dead last in EPA per play. With an unheralded backup commanding the offense this week, an already dismal situation gets even bleaker.

Fortunately for Los Angeles, the opponent traveling to SoFi Stadium this week will trot out its own backup quarterback. The Patriots are set to start Tommy DeVito while Drake Maye recovers from his fractured fibula.

#2474. Aaron Rodgers claims he was 'barred' from Steelers' facility: Why QB went scorched earth on Mike McCarthy

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Based on how they played Friday, it seems like the Pittsburgh Steelers have already put the Aaron Rodgers drama behind them, but the same can't be said for the four-time NFL MVP.

Rodgers has taken some heat this week for breaking the sanctity of the locker room and he decided to respond to that accusation by sending a text message to Al Michaels, who was on the call for Pittsburgh's Black Friday game against the Broncos.

During the fourth quarter of the Amazon Prime stream, Michaels read out loud what Rodgers had sent him.

"A lot of talk about the sanctity of the locker room," Michaels said of what Rodgers wrote. "The code or sanctity exists to protect the integrity of the locker room, not to provide immunity from accountability for its leadership. They took this public. Never heard from the head coach. Then they leaked at 11 p.m. They also barred me from the facility. That's why I went to [Pat] McAfee."

It's a short text, but there's a lot to unpack here.

For one, let's start with the fact Rodgers claims he was "barred'' from the team facility. The Steelers announced Rodgers' benching at 11:10 p.m. ET on Tuesday and they did that even though no one in the organization had actually spoken to Rodgers before the announcement came out (They did speak with his agent, though).

Steelers coach Mike McCarthy made the decision to bench Rodgers after the QB gave him an ultimatum at some point on Tuesday: relinquish play-calling duties or release him. Although Rodgers didn't get released at that point, that did lead to his benching.

The QB didn't show up for practice on Wednesday, and according to multiple reports, that was because the team had excused him from practice, but according to Rodgers, it was because he was banned from the facility.

The Steelers' decision to lock Rodgers out is why he ultimately chose to talk to Pat McAfee on Wednesday. The interview was a wild ride, with Rodgers throwing out multiple accusations at Mike McCarthy, including that he had missed meetings, fallen asleep during meetings and skipped walk-throughs.

Just hours after the interview with McAfee ended, Rodgers was released.

During Thursday's slate of Thanksgiving games, Rodgers was called out by Tom Brady for breaking the "sanctity" of the NFL locker room, and an accusation like that from Brady likely rubbed Rodgers the wrong way, which would explain why he used Brady's wording in his text to Michaels.

Based on Rodgers' claim, he may not have done the McAfee interview if he hadn't been barred from the facility, and if there had been no interview, this situation might have turned out differently. But it also seems Rodgers was determined to burn every bridge on his way out of town, so it's hard to say whether things would have turned out differently.

Either way, the Steelers have moved on from the former quarterback and they did so in dominant fashion by beating the Denver Broncos 27-5 on Friday.
